newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Maori protestors lower NZ flag on national day.
newsitem.headline: Maori protestors lower NZ flag on national day.

text.p: New Zealand Maori protestors seeking greater self-determination lowered the country's flag and raised their own at annual Waitangi Day celebrations here on Thursday.

But the national commemoration, held in hot sunshine on the site of the signing of the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi between British settlers and Maori chiefs, passed with only minor signs of dissent and without the confrontations common in past years. The official Waitangi Day events were moved to the capital Wellington from Waitangi in the far north two years ago after Maori protestors insulted diplomatic guests and one spat at the then-Governor General Dame Catherine Tizard.

A handful of police and security guards with dogs watched without intervening as the New Zealand flag and the Union Jack were lowered and replaced with various flags including the red, white and black flag of the Maori self-determination movement.

Maori, the original Polynesian settlers of New Zealand who reached the country by canoe around 1,000 years before white Europeans arrived in the 18th century, make up 13 percent of the nation's population.
The Treaty ensured British rule and cleared the way for further colonial settlement, while granting Maori British citizenship and rights to their lands, resources and "treasures".
Deputy Prime Minister and New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, himself of Maori extraction, attended an open air church service and watched Maori cultural groups perform at the treaty grounds.
Peters' New Zealand First Party won a clean sweep of the five seats set aside for Maori in the general election in October, ending the left-wing Labour Party's grip on the indigenous vote.
In December, he took New Zealand First into coalition government with the conservative National Party.

Together they promised a range of measures to improve the lot of the Maori, who are greatly over-represented in statistics for crime, poor education, unemployment and health problems, but are under-represented in positions of power.
Peters described the symbolic flag-lowering as "disappointing" and was critical of the church service being conducted mostly in Maori.
"The mass majority of Maori in this country support the New Zealand flag. They may not like its design or its look but it is the symbolism that they do support," Peters told Reuters.

Peters said the ceremony would return officially to Waitangi when the Maori elders of the region were prepared to defend the protocols. National Foreign Affairs Minister Don McKinnon said he hoped it would be back in Waitangi for the year 2000.
